reason: The sources thoroughly document the 1897 last stand with multiple cross-verified tactical details, communication logs, and aftermath commemorations across multiple independent sites.
story: On September 12, 1897, twenty-one Sikh soldiers of the British Indian Army's 36th Sikhs were garrisoned at Saragarhi, a small communication outpost on the North-West Frontier. Surrounded by an army of roughly ten thousand Pashtun tribesmen, the garrison commander, Havildar Ishar Singh, chose to hold the post to protect neighbouring Fort Lockhart and Fort Gulistan. Because Saragarhi was equipped with a heliograph mirror signalling system, signaller Sepoy Gurmukh Singh flashed real-time updates across the valley to commanding officers as wave after wave of attackers assaulted the walls. With relief blocked, the defenders held out for hours. When tribesmen breached the outer perimeter under a smokescreen, hand-to-hand fighting ensued. Gurmukh Singh sent his final message asking permission to stow the heliograph and take up his rifle before entering the fray. All twenty-one defenders fell, but their stand delayed the enemy and earned unanimous posthumous gallantry honours.
angle: As ten thousand enemy tribesmen breached their walls, the lone signaller paused during the battle to flash a heliograph mirror message across the valley asking permission to put down his communications gear and take up his rifle.

claims.claim: The Battle of Saragarhi took place on September 12, 1897, on the Samana Range of the North-West Frontier.
The Saragarhi garrison consisted of 21 Sikh soldiers belonging to the 36th Sikhs of the British Indian Army.
The defending garrison was commanded by Havildar Ishar Singh.
The attacking force consisted of approximately 10,000 or more Afridi and Orakzai Pashtun tribesmen.
Saragarhi served as a crucial heliograph signalling relay post between Fort Lockhart and Fort Gulistan.
The assault on the Saragarhi signalling post began around 9:00 AM.
Sepoy Gurmukh Singh operated the heliograph during the battle, sending live status reports to Fort Lockhart.
Lieutenant Colonel John Haughton at Fort Lockhart could not send immediate reinforcements to relieve Saragarhi.
Attackers created a smokescreen by setting fire to bushes and shrubs to approach and breach the wall.
Havildar Ishar Singh ordered his men to fall back into the inner defenses while covering their retreat.
Sepoy Gurmukh Singh requested permission via heliograph to pack his equipment and pick up his rifle before making his final stand.
Sepoy Gurmukh Singh's final words shouted during the defense included the Sikh battle cry 'Bole So Nihal, Sat Sri Akal'.
All 21 Sikh soldiers defending the post were killed in action during the battle.
The Pashtun attackers suffered heavy casualties, with estimates of around 180 to several hundred killed.
All 21 defenders were posthumously awarded the Indian Order of Merit, the highest gallantry award available to Indian soldiers at the time.
The British built two memorial gurdwaras to honor the fallen soldiers, located in Amritsar and Ferozepur.
The British Parliament rose in a standing ovation upon hearing the account of the garrison's stand.
Saragarhi Day is commemorated annually on September 12 by the Sikh Regiment.

disputed: The total number of tribal attackers varies across accounts from 6,000 to over 20,000; the script should attribute this as 'estimated at ten thousand or more'.
Attacker death counts range from around 180 admitted dead to 600 or more seen on the field; the script should frame this as 'suffering hundreds of casualties'.
The specific number of attackers killed by Sepoy Gurmukh Singh alone is stated as 20 in some accounts and 40 in others; the script should attribute this as 'according to regimental tradition'.
